proposals.label: Shared global rules of the road
proposals.definition: Calls for common international rules, safeguards, norms and possibly new institutions or a framework convention to govern AI.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages calling for common rules, safeguards, global guardrails, a framework convention, or IAEA/ITU-like institutions for AI.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude passages that only describe UN bodies without calling for rules.
proposals.boundary_cases: Proposals for a UN framework convention count here and in AI_UN_ROLE.

examples.quote: We must urgently establish common rules and safeguards for AI.
we must collectively formulate new rules and be prepared to create new institutions if necessary for new technologies

proposals.label: UN AI bodies as convergence venue
proposals.definition: Support for UN-specific AI processes (High-Level Advisory Body, Scientific Panel, Global Dialogue, Global Digital Compact, OEWG) and the UN as the universal venue for AI norms.
proposals.inclusion: Include welcomes of UN AI bodies/reports and claims that the UN has a critical role in AI governance.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude calls for rules that name no UN body or role.
proposals.boundary_cases: Lessons from the ICT OEWG applied to AI count here.

examples.quote: Singapore welcomes the report of the High-Level Advisory Body on AI
The UN, the United Nations, has a critical role to play in building convergence

proposals.label: Loss of control and frontier AI safeguards
proposals.definition: Technical AI safety concerns: loss of control of autonomous systems, WMD misuse by rogue actors, testing and evaluation, incident reporting, human control.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages on loss of control, testing/evaluation before deployment, frontier model safety, or keeping humans in control.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude battlefield or nuclear command uses of AI (AI_MILITARY_WEAPONS) unless framed as general safety.
proposals.boundary_cases: The 'nuclear button' thought experiment is used to illustrate human control generally; code here and AI_MILITARY_WEAPONS.

examples.quote: First, the loss of control of autonomous systems.
We need rigorous testing and evaluation before deployment.

proposals.label: AI in conflict and nuclear escalation
proposals.definition: Risks of AI in conflict situations and nuclear decision-making, raising miscalculation and escalation risk.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages on AI in conflict, military systems, or control of nuclear weapons.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude general loss-of-control safety concerns not tied to conflict.
proposals.boundary_cases: Rogue actors using AI for bioweapons is closer to AI_SAFETY_EXISTENTIAL/misuse than state military use.

examples.quote: the advent of artificial intelligence in conflict situations has actually increased the risks exponentially
Do you want the nuclear button to be in the hands of a human being or an AI?

proposals.label: Powerful engine needs good brakes
proposals.definition: Framing AI as both extraordinary potential and peril, requiring innovation and safeguards together.
proposals.inclusion: Include explicit promise/peril pairings or engine-and-brakes metaphors.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude one-sided benefit or risk statements.
proposals.boundary_cases: Where the duality leads to a governance call, code both.

examples.quote: By now, the promises and the perils of AI are well known to all of us.
every powerful engine needs good brakes, safeguards

proposals.label: Skills-driven AI productivity gains
proposals.definition: AI as a productivity engine requiring investment in skills, talent and infrastructure so workers and businesses can redesign work.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages on productivity gains from AI and equipping workers with AI skills.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude capacity support to other countries (AI_CAPACITY_BUILDING).
proposals.boundary_cases: Domestic skills investment for small states may also be AI_NATIONAL_STRATEGY.

examples.quote: The real productivity gains from AI comes not from the IT department, but from our businesses and workers having the skills

proposals.label: AI eroding trust, outpacing governance
proposals.definition: AI framed as a monumental, fast-moving disruption that outpaces existing governance and makes building trust in technology the central challenge.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages emphasizing the speed/scale of AI disruption, lost trust in technology, or inadequacy of existing rules.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude passages focused only on specific harms like weapons or disinformation.
proposals.boundary_cases: If the passage moves to calls for global rules, also code AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE.

examples.quote: It appears to be moving far too fast for anybody, let alone governments, to manage to keep pace.
I am afraid that in our digital age, part of the problem of losing trust lies with science and technology.

proposals.label: Collective global rules for AI
proposals.definition: Calls for collectively set global rules on AI, since no state can manage it alone, including governance that balances opportunity and risk with private sector commitment.
proposals.inclusion: Include calls for global/international AI rules or collective governance involving all actors.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude statements that only describe AI's speed without a governance call.
proposals.boundary_cases: References to the Global Digital Compact or SG advisory body also get AI_UN_ROLE.

examples.quote: acknowledging that the rules need to be set globally and they need to be stuck to even as they develop
We need to find a way to govern the development of new technologies, including artificial intelligence

proposals.label: Human-centric, rights-based lifecycle approach
proposals.definition: A human-centric and human rights-based approach across the full technology life cycle.
proposals.inclusion: Include calls for human-centric or rights-based AI approaches.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude general trust concerns without a rights/values framing.
proposals.boundary_cases: Appeals to 'the right values' underpinning action are borderline; include only when values are human-centred.

examples.quote: The answer should be a humancentric and human rights-based approach to the full life cycle of technologies

proposals.label: SG advisory body and Global Digital Compact
proposals.definition: Support for UN AI processes such as the SG's high-level advisory body on AI and the Global Digital Compact.
proposals.inclusion: Include mentions of UN AI bodies or the Global Digital Compact.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude non-UN governance calls.
proposals.boundary_cases: Split passages that complete a sentence about the SG advisory body count.

examples.quote: I applaud the Secretary- General’s resolve to form a high-level advisory body on
The Global Digital Compact should be centred on that notion.

proposals.label: AI useful but dangerous
proposals.definition: AI explicitly framed as both useful and dangerous.
proposals.inclusion: Include explicit dual framings of AI.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude one-sided framings.
proposals.boundary_cases: Governance that 'does not impede opportunities and does not put us at risk' also qualifies.

examples.quote: Artificial intelligence can be useful, but it can also be dangerous.

proposals.label: International rules to secure public confidence
proposals.definition: International rules grounded in international law are called for so the public can trust that AI will enhance rather than destroy humanity.
proposals.inclusion: Include calls for international AI rules framed around public trust or international law.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude digital security threats (cyber attacks, cable cutting) that are not linked to AI.
proposals.boundary_cases: The phrase 'enhance and not destroy humanity' alludes to catastrophic fears but the passage's claim is about rules, so code here rather than AI_SAFETY_EXISTENTIAL.

examples.quote: If we are to stand any chance of securing public confidence that AI can enhance and not destroy humanity, we need a set of international rules that reflect international law.

proposals.label: Support for Global Digital Compact implementation
proposals.definition: Support for implementing the Global Digital Compact and wider UN digital cooperation efforts.
proposals.inclusion: Include endorsements of the Global Digital Compact or UN digital cooperation in an AI context.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude general UN reform appeals without digital/AI content.
proposals.boundary_cases: Cyber resilience and cable protection within the same passage are generic digital security and not coded as AI unless AI is named.

examples.quote: Malta, my country, wholeheartedly supports the implementation of the Global Digital Compact and wider UN efforts to strengthen international digital cooperation

proposals.label: AI algorithms harming children's mental health
proposals.definition: AI-driven algorithms, social media and chatbots framed as harming children's and teenagers' mental health, with calls for health-and-safety style regulation and age limits.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages on AI-optimized social media, chatbots or algorithms harming minors, and on age verification, phone bans or platform duty of care for children.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude general youth education or AI skills passages that do not concern harm to children.
proposals.boundary_cases: Passages about social media harms without explicit AI mention count when they continue an argument where AI-driven algorithms were named.

examples.quote: Social media algorithms are constantly improved by AI to keep children online for the maximum amount of time
We don't want our kids to share their intimate thoughts and feelings with an AI chatbot.
Digital technology is no different than any other industry that needs to operate under health and safety regulations.
The brains of our children are being rewired, and their development changed on an almost unimaginable scale.

proposals.label: Unaccountable power of big tech companies
proposals.definition: Concern that a few large technology companies wield more power than states and are not accountable.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages about tech companies' outsized economic power, lack of accountability, or AI concentrating power in few corporations.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude passages about state-level digital divides without corporate power framing.
proposals.boundary_cases: Calls for tech companies to join governance processes fit here and in AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE.

examples.quote: a few very large technology companies, with more economic muscle than most of the countries represented here
concentrate immense power in the hands of a few multinational corporations

proposals.label: Global framework like a COP for AI
proposals.definition: Calls to put AI regulation on a global footing, e.g. a conference of the parties for AI modeled on climate governance.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages proposing global regimes, COP-style frameworks or agile global governance for AI.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude national regulatory measures only (e.g. school phone bans).
proposals.boundary_cases: Praise of UN advisory body reports fits here and in AI_UN_ROLE.

examples.quote: Eventually, what we may need is a conference of the parties for AI, with the participation not just of countries but also of the global technology companies.
with AI there is no such framework

proposals.label: Support for UN AI bodies and reports
proposals.definition: Endorsement of UN AI institutions: SG High-Level Advisory Body report, Scientific Panel, Global Dialogue, Global Digital Compact.
proposals.inclusion: Include explicit praise or welcome of named UN AI bodies, reports or compacts.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude generic references to multilateralism.
proposals.boundary_cases: If the UN mention is only a conditional ('if the GDC is to have effect') it still counts.

examples.quote: I welcome the United Nations establishment of the independent international scientific panel on AI and the global dialogue on artificial intelligence governance.
presented just a few days ago by the High-Level Advisory Body on Artificial Intelligence, established by the Secretary- General

proposals.label: Transformative promise versus extraordinary harm
proposals.definition: AI presented as a game-changing general-purpose technology with great benefits but also capacity for extraordinary harm (deepfakes, control, job displacement).
proposals.inclusion: Include passages explicitly weighing AI's transformative benefits against its dangers.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude passages that only describe harms to children.
proposals.boundary_cases: Deepfake/disinformation mentions within the duality framing can also be coded AI_DISINFORMATION.

examples.quote: However, AI also has the potential to do extraordinary harm.
generative AI is used to create more and more convincing deepfakes, designed to spread misinformation and disinformation

proposals.label: Greek AI pilots in public services
proposals.definition: Description of the country's own AI strategy and pilots in education, health, and disaster prevention.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages describing national AI programmes or deployments.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude hypothetical benefits not tied to national action.
proposals.boundary_cases: National child-safety tools (Kids Wallet) belong to AI_CHILD_PROTECTION rather than here.

examples.quote: Greece is pursuing a visionary yet practical AI strategy through pilot programs in areas such as education, healthcare, and natural disaster prevention.

proposals.label: Regulatory framework so AI serves good
proposals.definition: Call for an appropriate regulatory framework to ensure AI and generative AI serve good rather than evil purposes.
proposals.inclusion: Include calls for regulatory frameworks for AI to steer it toward beneficial use.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude statements about AI being neglected without a regulatory call.
proposals.boundary_cases: Support for the Secretary-General's actions alongside regulatory calls is also coded AI_UN_ROLE.

examples.quote: then an appropriate framework for regulatory action must be put in place

proposals.label: Support for Secretary-General's AI actions
proposals.definition: Endorsement of the UN Secretary-General's actions on AI.
proposals.inclusion: Include expressions of support for SG or UN initiatives on AI.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude non-UN governance calls.
proposals.boundary_cases: Implicit reference to SG actions following an AI regulation sentence counts here.

examples.quote: We therefore support the actions of the Secretary- General

proposals.label: AI and preserving democracy
proposals.definition: Framing AI governance as a test of whether democracy is preserved or allowed to crumble.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages linking AI to the survival or erosion of democracy.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude election-specific disinformation claims (AI_DISINFORMATION) unless democracy's survival is the frame.
proposals.boundary_cases: Rhetorical questions about future judgement on democracy count when tied to AI.

examples.quote: whether we sought to preserve our democracy or whether we allowed it to crumble

proposals.label: AI overshadowed by climate crisis
proposals.definition: Observation that AI receives insufficient attention because other crises (climate) dominate the agenda.
proposals.inclusion: Include statements that AI is not a focal point or is crowded out by other priorities.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude lists of crises that merely include AI.
proposals.boundary_cases: If the speaker uses neglect to argue for urgent regulation, code both this and AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE.

examples.quote: AI is not in the immediate focal point of many because the drama and the crises that surround climate are taking up all of the oxygen

proposals.label: AI replacing human intellect and jobs
proposals.definition: Concern that AI, unlike earlier automation of physical tasks, replaces intellectual work with devastating job-market consequences.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages about AI replacing human intellectual capacities or labour and resulting unemployment.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude general poverty/unemployment statements not linked to AI.
proposals.boundary_cases: Job-loss arguments that end in wealth-concentration claims are also coded AI_SOVEREIGNTY_CONCENTRATION.

examples.quote: today the human intellect risks being replaced, with consequences that could be devastating, particularly for the job market

proposals.label: Concentration of power and wealth
proposals.definition: Concern that AI-driven change concentrates power and wealth in the hands of a few, making people unnecessary.
proposals.inclusion: Include statements linking AI to concentration of power or wealth among few actors.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude inter-state access gaps without concentration language (AI_DIGITAL_DIVIDE).
proposals.boundary_cases: Domestic-inequality framing still counts if concentration of power/wealth is explicit.

examples.quote: a world ever-dominated by disparities and by the concentration of power and wealth in the hands of the few

proposals.label: Great opportunities, enormous inherent risks
proposals.definition: AI presented as seemingly beneficial but carrying enormous inherent risks, with development outpacing capacity to manage it.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages explicitly contrasting AI's opportunities with its inherent risks or pace outstripping management.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude one-sided statements.
proposals.boundary_cases: Pace-of-change concerns without opportunity framing may go to AI_SAFETY_EXISTENTIAL if loss of control is implied.

examples.quote: may offer great opportunities in many fields, but we cannot pretend to not understand its enormous inherent risks
whose pace is much faster than our capacity to manage its effects

proposals.label: Widening gap between possibility and reality
proposals.definition: AI's promise for human well-being contrasted with peoples facing starvation and war, as if living in two different eras.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages contrasting AI's possibilities with global deprivation and inequality between peoples.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude labour-market arguments within one country.
proposals.boundary_cases: AI named with genetics as a frontier of possibility, if not contrasted with deprivation, is AI_TECH_LIST_MENTION.

examples.quote: In areas such as genetics and artificial intelligence, the possibilities for realizing the well-being of all humanity are increasing. But the gap between possibility and reality is also widening.

proposals.label: AI among exciting new technologies
proposals.definition: AI is named within a list of emerging technologies (robotics, 3D printing, Internet of Things) as a source of possible solutions, without further discussion.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages where AI appears only as one item among listed technologies or trends.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude passages that develop an argument specifically about AI.
proposals.boundary_cases: If the list is used to make an inequality point, code AI_DIGITAL_DIVIDE as well.

examples.quote: from advanced robotics and artificial intelligence to 3D printing and the Internet of things

proposals.label: Technological inequality in access to AI
proposals.definition: AI and related technologies are experienced by only part of the world; fighting technological inequality is framed as a development goal.
proposals.inclusion: Include statements that only some countries or people can access AI and related technologies.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude pure technology lists with no inequality claim.
proposals.boundary_cases: Link to the SDGs is coded here rather than AI_DEVELOPMENT_SDGS when the focus is inequality.

examples.quote: big data, artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things are concepts — terms — that only a part of the world can experience
Inequality includes technological inequality.

proposals.label: Countering public fear of AI
proposals.definition: Acknowledges public anxiety about AI (machines taking over, job loss, loss of control) and counters it by asserting that right leadership decisions can make AI's impact positive.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages that address public fear, media alarmism or anxiety about AI and offer reassurance.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude passages that themselves warn of catastrophic AI risk (AI_SAFETY_EXISTENTIAL).
proposals.boundary_cases: Mentions of job-loss fears framed as media alarmism are coded here, not AI_ECONOMY_LABOR, unless labour impacts are analysed.

examples.quote: lurid media headlines about the machines taking over, spreading fear about AI taking jobs and rendering human effort obsolete
harness the power of AI for the public and common good, not fear it as a coming catastrophe

proposals.label: National AI pilots in public services
proposals.definition: The speaker describes its own AI pilot projects enhancing public services such as health care and traffic management.
proposals.inclusion: Include descriptions of the speaker country's AI projects or leadership.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude calls for global action without national detail.
proposals.boundary_cases: Small-state framing of limited national capacity leading to global cooperation calls is also coded AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE.

examples.quote: We have six pilot projects covering areas from health care to traffic management.

proposals.label: Global action to make AI global good
proposals.definition: Calls for enhanced international cooperation on AI because no single country can manage it alone.
proposals.inclusion: Include calls for international cooperation or global action on AI.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude national pilot descriptions.
proposals.boundary_cases: Cooperation calls without regulatory content still count here.

examples.quote: To make AI a global good, we need global action.

proposals.label: Legal rules against AI weaponization
proposals.definition: Calls for legal rules to prevent the weaponization of AI as part of new governance structures for emerging domains.
proposals.inclusion: Passages calling for legal rules or norms preventing AI weaponization.
proposals.exclusion: Cyberspace or outer space norms without AI (not AI themes).
proposals.boundary_cases: When AI weaponization is one item among cyber and space norms, code this plus AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE.

examples.quote: forming legal rules that will prevent the weaponization of artificial intelligence

proposals.label: New structures for emerging technologies
proposals.definition: Need for new international structures and norms to govern rapid advances in emerging domains, including AI.
proposals.inclusion: Passages calling for new global structures/norms covering AI among other domains.
proposals.exclusion: National governance frameworks alone (use AI_NATIONAL_STRATEGY).
proposals.boundary_cases: National preparation paired with global structures counts here for the global part.

examples.quote: we need new structures to govern rapid advances in other areas

proposals.label: AI benefits for health and development
proposals.definition: AI presented as delivering concrete benefits in health, science and development, including partnerships to share these benefits with developing countries.
proposals.inclusion: Passages citing AI speeding cancer diagnosis, drug discovery, AI for development partnerships in Africa or SDG ecosystems.
proposals.exclusion: Economic growth/productivity framing without health or development content (use AI_ECONOMY_LABOR).
proposals.boundary_cases: Donor-funded AI ecosystem programmes abroad count here and may also count as AI_CAPACITY_BUILDING.

examples.quote: In our National Health Service, AI mammogram trials double the speed of diagnosis.
working with 10 African partners creating AI ecosystems that empower thousands of communities to meet the sustainable development goals
not just to help prevent and treat cancer, but to help cure it

proposals.label: AI growth, jobs and worker disruption
proposals.definition: AI as a driver of productivity and growth and as a source of labour disruption requiring support for workers, including industrial-revolution analogies.
proposals.inclusion: Passages on AI productivity gains, reindustrialisation, jobs of the future, or protecting workers through disruption.
proposals.exclusion: Health or SDG applications (use AI_DEVELOPMENT_SDGS).
proposals.boundary_cases: National investment in AI industries to create jobs counts here and in AI_NATIONAL_STRATEGY.

examples.quote: AI will also be a source of disruption to the way we live and work, a multiplier of risk.
we are driving investment in industries of the future to create new jobs, from low-carbon technologies to artificial intelligence

proposals.label: AI-enabled disinformation and propaganda
proposals.definition: AI used by hostile states and actors to spread propaganda, manipulate information and amplify disinformation.
proposals.inclusion: Passages on AI fuelling disinformation, chatbots manipulated to repeat propaganda, or AI multiplying information threats.
proposals.exclusion: AI-enabled financial scams and crime without an information-manipulation focus (use AI_CYBER_SECURITY).
proposals.boundary_cases: A passage where AI is said to multiply the threat of disinformation and cyber attacks together can take both codes.

examples.quote: Authoritarian states, notably Russia, are manipulating large-scale, large model language models so that chatbots answer in the voice of their propaganda
we have seen cyber attacks on companies and institutions, and we know that AI will multiply the threat

proposals.label: AI misuse by criminals and security threats
proposals.definition: AI used for crime, scams, repression, or threats to critical infrastructure, and AI as a security tool to defend against them.
proposals.inclusion: Passages on criminals using AI for scams, AI empowering crime, or AI defence partnerships to protect critical infrastructure.
proposals.exclusion: Autonomous weapons or battlefield AI (use AI_MILITARY_WEAPONS).
proposals.boundary_cases: Defensive AI for national infrastructure counts here rather than military weapons.

examples.quote: Organised crime is using AI to supercharge their scams, deceiving victims on an unprecedented scale.
we are developing a new AI defense partnership with the United States to protect our critical national infrastructure

proposals.label: Frontier AI safety and preparedness
proposals.definition: Concern with frontier AI safety, investing in AI safety/security institutes, and global standards to ensure safe AI development.
proposals.inclusion: Passages mentioning AI Security/Safety Institutes, safe AI development, frontier AI risks and preparedness.
proposals.exclusion: Crime or disinformation misuse (use those codes).
proposals.boundary_cases: Calls for global safety standards take both this and AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE.

examples.quote: we have our world-leading AI Security Institute, working hand in glove with the US and the leading labs on AI safety
to ensure that AI development is safe

proposals.label: Global AI principles via G20 and UN
proposals.definition: Calls for shared global principles and standards on AI through G20, UN processes and cooperation, including endorsement of UN AI bodies.
proposals.inclusion: Passages proposing global AI principles/standards, putting AI at the heart of a G20 presidency, or welcoming UN AI governance dialogue and scientific panel.
proposals.exclusion: Purely domestic regulation (use AI_NATIONAL_STRATEGY).
proposals.boundary_cases: Welcoming the UN Scientific Panel and Global Dialogue should also be coded AI_UN_ROLE.

examples.quote: we will work towards agreeing a single set of global principles and standards
I commend the new independent international scientific panel on AI

proposals.label: Sharing AI benefits to avoid inequality
proposals.definition: Concern that AI benefits are concentrated and must be shared globally to prevent deeper inequality.
proposals.inclusion: Passages urging investment and partnership so AI benefits reach those who need them, or warning technological change could deepen inequality.
proposals.exclusion: Concentration of power framed as sovereignty/dependence (use AI_SOVEREIGNTY_CONCENTRATION).
proposals.boundary_cases: Digital access programmes narrowing the technological divide count here.

examples.quote: we risk a world of ever deeper inequality, where the benefits of this technology fail to reach those who need it most
the risk that technological change could become a source of inequality and division rather than the greatest opportunity in history

proposals.label: Own-country AI leadership and investment
proposals.definition: Speaker showcases own country's AI talent, institutions, investment and national leadership role.
proposals.inclusion: Passages boasting national AI talent, institutes, datasets or national-level AI investments and initiatives.
proposals.exclusion: International proposals for common rules (use AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE).
proposals.boundary_cases: Announcing a national G20 agenda on AI counts as both national positioning and global governance.

examples.quote: The UK has some of the best tech and AI talent anywhere in the world.
we invest so heavily in the AI Security Institute, with more dedicated researchers than anywhere else in the world

proposals.label: AI can empower freedom or repression
proposals.definition: Explicit framing of AI as both a defining opportunity and a profound challenge whose direction depends on choices.
proposals.inclusion: Passages contrasting AI's potential to empower good versus harm.
proposals.exclusion: One-sided benefit or risk passages.
proposals.boundary_cases: Describing frontier AI as one of the most significant challenges and opportunities counts.

examples.quote: AI can empower freedom or it can entrench repression. AI can empower truth or it can entrench lies.
one of the most significant challenges and opportunities of our age, frontier AI

proposals.label: Frontier AI, superintelligence and misalignment
proposals.definition: Concern about frontier or agentic AI that may surpass human intelligence, is not understood by its creators, and poses risks of misuse, misadventure or misalignment with human objectives.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages on superintelligence, loss of understanding or control, misalignment, or frontier AI risks.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude military autonomous weapons (AI_MILITARY_WEAPONS) and ordinary criminal misuse (AI_CYBER_SECURITY).
proposals.boundary_cases: A company race toward superintelligence is coded here when the risk is the capability itself, and also AI_SOVEREIGNTY_CONCENTRATION if corporate power is stressed.

examples.quote: The principal risks of frontier AI will therefore come from misuse, misadventure or misalignment with human objectives.
the stated aim of those companies is to build superintelligence, AI that strives
to surpass intelligence in every possible way. Some people working on that think it is just a few years away.

proposals.label: New multilateralism and AI safety summits
proposals.definition: Calls for international cooperation, a new form of multilateralism and summits to build shared understanding of AI risks and make AI safe.
proposals.inclusion: Include calls for international action, shared risk understanding, or summit processes on AI safety or governance.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude endorsements of specific UN bodies only (AI_UN_ROLE).
proposals.boundary_cases: Statements on the importance of democratic rule-based cultures for safe AI may be coded here or AI_DEMOCRATIC_VALUES.

examples.quote: that challenge requires a new form of multilateralism — because it is only by working together that we will make AI safe for everyone

proposals.label: Company races and power of few
proposals.definition: Concern that AI is driven by a competitive race among companies and countries, that tech firms hold country-sized influence, and that decisions should not be left to a few.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages on corporate or state competition over AI, the outsized influence of tech companies, or decisions being concentrated in few hands.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude access-gap framings about developing countries (AI_DIGITAL_DIVIDE).
proposals.boundary_cases: Applause for voluntary company safety commitments alongside race concerns is coded here.

examples.quote: the starting gun has been fired on a globally competitive race in which individual companies, as well as countries, will strive to push the boundaries as far and fast as possible
ensure that decisions about artificial intelligence are not left in the hands of a few

proposals.label: Democratizing tool that can be misused
proposals.definition: AI framed as a democratizing, empowering tool for all that can equally be used for ill, requiring both benefit-sharing and risk preparation.
proposals.inclusion: Include explicit pairing of AI's empowering potential with its dangers.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude risk-only or benefit-only statements.
proposals.boundary_cases: Calls to both prepare for risks and distribute benefits fairly count here and may also be AI_DIGITAL_DIVIDE.

examples.quote: AI can and should be a tool for all. Yet any technology that can be used by all can also be used for ill.
we must not only prepare for the risks of those technologies but also distribute their benefits more fairly

proposals.label: Criminal, terrorist and state misuse of AI
proposals.definition: Examples of AI already being misused by hackers, terrorists, cybercriminals with deepfakes, and repressive states.
proposals.inclusion: Include concrete examples of AI misuse for crime, terrorism, election manipulation, or repression.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude hypothetical frontier misalignment risks (AI_SAFETY_EXISTENTIAL).
proposals.boundary_cases: Deepfakes used to dupe voters also qualify for AI_DISINFORMATION.

examples.quote: teens hacking individuals’ bank details, terrorists targeting Government systems, cybercriminals duping voters with deepfakes and bots, even States suppressing their peoples

proposals.label: Autonomous weapons already in use
proposals.definition: Observation that autonomous weapons without human control are already used in current wars.
proposals.inclusion: Include references to autonomous weapons or AI in warfare.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude non-military AI agent concerns.
proposals.boundary_cases: AI agents transacting with humans are not military and belong to AI_TRANSFORMATIVE_SIGNIFICANCE.

examples.quote: autonomous weapons systems without human fingers on the triggers are already with us — witness the wars around us

proposals.label: AI as defining test of era
proposals.definition: AI presented as an epochal transformation or defining leadership test with profound implications for societies, politics and economies, including AI agents indistinguishable from humans.
proposals.inclusion: Include rhetorical framings of AI as the greatest test, a revolution, or a profound societal shift without specifying a policy domain.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude passages whose main point is a specific risk or governance proposal.
proposals.boundary_cases: A one-sentence statement of AI's importance with no further content is coded here rather than AI_TECH_LIST_MENTION because AI is singled out.

examples.quote: In the years ahead, there may well be no greater test of our leadership than how we deal with AI.
AI agents with the ability to negotiate and transact with each other and humans, and often we will not be able to tell the difference

proposals.label: Support for SG AI Advisory Body
proposals.definition: Support for the recommendations of the Secretary-General's High-level Advisory Body on AI.
proposals.inclusion: Include endorsements of UN AI bodies or their recommendations.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude national or G7 summit processes.
proposals.boundary_cases: If paired with 'not in the hands of a few', also code AI_SOVEREIGNTY_CONCENTRATION.

examples.quote: We must support those recommendations and move forward with that common effort

proposals.label: Democratic openness as basis for safe AI
proposals.definition: Argument that liberal democracies with open expression, rules and transparency are best placed to build AI capacity and make AI safe.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages linking democratic values, openness, or transparency to AI innovation and safety.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude human-rights-of-users arguments (AI_HUMAN_RIGHTS_ETHICS).
proposals.boundary_cases: Mentions of states using AI to suppress people are coded AI_CYBER_SECURITY unless contrasted with democratic AI.

examples.quote: A culture of rules and transparency is essential to creativity and innovation, and it is just as essential to making AI safe.

proposals.label: AI-driven manipulation and election interference
proposals.definition: AI and algorithms used to fabricate, personalize and amplify false narratives that manipulate citizens and elections.
proposals.inclusion: Passages describing AI-generated or algorithmically amplified lies, micro-targeted propaganda, or election interference.
proposals.exclusion: General complaints about state fear-mongering or media without reference to AI or algorithmic amplification.
proposals.boundary_cases: Discussion of 'reach' and platform amplification counts when automation or machines are named as the amplifier.

examples.quote: The algorithm did not invent the objective. A human actor did. The algorithm did not develop hatred. It discovered how to activate ours.
Reach can be purchased. automated, manipulated, and secretly assigned by platforms, corporations, criminal networks, and foreign states.

proposals.label: Human agency and accountability over AI
proposals.definition: Insistence that humans retain judgment, responsibility and legal accountability for decisions assisted by AI, and warnings against cognitive outsourcing to machines.
proposals.inclusion: Passages arguing that AI must strengthen rather than replace human judgment, or that a named human must answer for AI-assisted decisions.
proposals.exclusion: Generic human-rights or ethics language about AI without the accountability/agency focus.
proposals.boundary_cases: Rhetoric that 'the machine will obey' counts when it frames humans as responsible for AI outcomes.

examples.quote: No machine possesses democratic legitimacy. No algorithm inherits constitutional responsibility.
We should not fear that machines will become too human. We should fear that human beings will become invisible behind machines.

proposals.label: Sovereign AI capability for small nations
proposals.definition: Concern that nations, especially small ones, depend on foreign or commercial AI systems they cannot inspect, and calls for sovereign AI capacity.
proposals.inclusion: Passages calling for national or allied AI capability so countries are not dependent on distant commercial operators.
proposals.exclusion: Passages only describing domestic AI projects without the dependence/sovereignty argument.
proposals.boundary_cases: Calls for an international compact on sovereign AI also fit governance; code both if dependence is explicit.

examples.quote: Sovereign artificial intelligence does not mean isolation. It means that no nation should be helpless before systems it cannot understand
Let us ensure that no small nation is forced to rent its understanding of reality from beyond its borders.

proposals.label: Rejecting AI pauses and preemptive regulation
proposals.definition: Arguments against moratoria or preemptive AI regulation, favouring acceleration, light-touch legal frameworks and Western/allied leadership.
proposals.inclusion: Passages opposing slowing or regulating AI in advance, or promoting deregulation and incentives to attract AI development.
proposals.exclusion: Passages calling for binding international rules or safety regulation of AI.
proposals.boundary_cases: Speakers who reject a pause but still demand accountability rules (e.g. accelerate with direction) fit here and may also fit governance themes.

examples.quote: a commitment not to regulate preemptively, limited liability for companies operating with AI agents and tax incentives
We cannot regulate ourselves into helplessness.

proposals.label: National AI initiatives and ambitions
proposals.definition: Speaker's own country's AI deployments, tools or ambitions to become an AI hub.
proposals.inclusion: Passages naming national AI projects (e.g. AI minister, AI detection tools) or national plans to attract AI investment.
proposals.exclusion: Abstract discussion of AI without reference to the speaker's own country's actions.
proposals.boundary_cases: A national tool described mainly as a counter-disinformation measure can be coded with both this and disinformation.

examples.quote: Albania became the first country to bring an artificial intelligence instrument into the architecture of government through Diella
we want to become the most competitive place in the world in which to develop it

proposals.label: AI as utopian or dystopian future
proposals.definition: Framing AI as an uncertain technology that could bring great benefits or great harms.
proposals.inclusion: Passages contrasting beneficial and catastrophic visions of AI or emerging technologies.
proposals.exclusion: Passages that discuss only harms or only benefits.
proposals.boundary_cases: Rhetorical questions posing AI as helper vs. terminator count here even without policy prescriptions.

examples.quote: Helpful robots washing and caring for an ageing population? Or pink-eyed terminators sent back from the future to cull the human race?

proposals.label: Reality falsification and deception
proposals.definition: Emerging technologies worsen risks of reality falsification, disinformation and deceptive ploys.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages on technology-enabled falsification of reality, disinformation or deception.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude privacy or plagiarism risks absent an information-integrity element.
proposals.boundary_cases: Lists of several risks can be coded here and to other themes simultaneously.

examples.quote: the worsening risks in terms of reality falsification
the spiralling effect of disinformation and ploys aimed at deception

proposals.label: Invasion of personal privacy
proposals.definition: Technology risks to personal privacy.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages on privacy invasion by emerging technologies.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude disinformation-only concerns.
proposals.boundary_cases: Data protection in cyberspace regulation calls may also be AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE.

examples.quote: invasion of personal privacy

proposals.label: Plagiarism disrupting education
proposals.definition: Generative technologies disrupting the educational process by facilitating plagiarism.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages on AI undermining education integrity, e.g., plagiarism or cheating.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude positive AI-in-education initiatives (AI_YOUTH_EDUCATION).
proposals.boundary_cases: Mixed statements on AI education benefits and cheating risks get both codes.

examples.quote: educational process disruption through the facilitation of plagiarism

proposals.label: Regulating cyberspace under international law
proposals.definition: Calls to unify efforts to prevent misuse and regulate technology/cyberspace based on international law, alongside cooperation and investment.
proposals.inclusion: Include calls for international regulation of technology misuse based on international law.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude calls only to encourage technological development.
proposals.boundary_cases: Cyberspace regulation framed around crime may also be AI_CYBER_SECURITY.

examples.quote: we reiterate the call for unifying efforts to prevent the misuse of cyberspace and regulate this vital aspect, based on the provisions of international law

proposals.label: Encouraging tech development and removing barriers
proposals.definition: Encouraging scientific development, cooperation and investment, and removing barriers between countries in technology.
proposals.inclusion: Include calls for cooperation, investment, or removal of cross-country barriers in technology development.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude risk-only passages.
proposals.boundary_cases: Calls to 'keep pace' with technology without cooperation framing are borderline; include when barriers or investment are mentioned.

examples.quote: encourage barriers between countries in this field to be removed

proposals.label: Rules and limits on autonomous weapons
proposals.definition: Calls for international rules and limits on autonomous weapon systems, given catastrophic harm if military use of new technologies is unchecked.
proposals.inclusion: Include calls for rules, limits or bans on autonomous weapons or unchecked military use of emerging technologies.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude civilian responsible-use norms for AI (AI_GLOBAL_GOVERNANCE).
proposals.boundary_cases: The phrase 'catastrophic harm' tied to military use is coded here, not AI_SAFETY_EXISTENTIAL.

examples.quote: We must commit to international rules and limits on autonomous weapon systems
the threat of catastrophic harm if their development and military use is left unchecked

proposals.label: Norms for responsible use of AI
proposals.definition: Calls for clear international norms on the responsible use of new and emerging technologies including AI.
proposals.inclusion: Include calls for norms or rules on responsible AI use.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude generic cyber or online extremism coalitions not linked to AI.
proposals.boundary_cases: Multistakeholder coalitions on cyberthreats in the same passage are digital, not AI, and are not coded here.

examples.quote: technologies, including artificial intelligence, as well as the continued peaceful use of outer space

proposals.label: Fears and uncertainties but new opportunities
proposals.definition: The AI revolution acknowledged as bringing fears and uncertainties but framed primarily as an opportunity for a better world if designed to serve everyone.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages pairing AI-related fears with opportunities, especially with an optimistic, conditional emphasis.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude passages that specify concrete risks or governance mechanisms.
proposals.boundary_cases: The 'designed to serve everyone' condition may also indicate AI_DIGITAL_DIVIDE if inequality is elaborated; here it is not.

examples.quote: The digital economy and the artificial-intelligence revolution bring with them fears and uncertainties, but above all they offer new opportunities for a better world

proposals.label: AI within prosperity and innovation agenda
proposals.definition: AI situated in a pro-market narrative of prosperity, entrepreneurship, innovation and trade.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages linking AI to economic prosperity, entrepreneurship and the digital economy.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude labour-disruption warnings without an economic-growth frame.
proposals.boundary_cases: Brief digital economy mentions count only when AI is explicitly named.

examples.quote: We want a more prosperous world, with more shared development and the freedom to be entrepreneurial and to innovate, create and trade.

proposals.label: Universally agreed legal frameworks for AI
proposals.definition: Calls for universally agreed legal frameworks covering AI alongside cybersecurity, lethal autonomous weapons and outer space.
proposals.inclusion: Include calls for universal or multilateral legal frameworks that explicitly cover AI.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude framework calls limited to cybersecurity or space without AI.
proposals.boundary_cases: Where lethal autonomous weapons are listed in the same call, also code AI_MILITARY_WEAPONS.

examples.quote: It is essential to develop universally agreed legal frameworks in the area of cybersecurity, lethal autonomous weapons systems, artificial intelligence and the weaponization of outer space.

proposals.label: Lethal autonomous weapons regulation
proposals.definition: Lethal autonomous weapons systems named as an area requiring legal frameworks.
proposals.inclusion: Include mentions of LAWS or military AI as subjects for regulation.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude civilian AI governance without military reference.
proposals.boundary_cases: A brief list item naming LAWS still counts here because the military application is explicit.

examples.quote: lethal autonomous weapons systems

proposals.label: Balancing misuse prevention with developing-country access
proposals.definition: A balance is sought between guarding against misuse of emerging technologies and facilitating developing countries' access to them.
proposals.inclusion: Include passages insisting that technology controls must not block developing-country access.
proposals.exclusion: Exclude pure misuse or security concerns without an access dimension.
proposals.boundary_cases: The passage refers to 'emerging technologies' generally; code as AI-related because AI is named in the same argument.

examples.quote: strike a prudent balance between guarding against the misuse of emerging technologies and facilitating access to them on the part of developing countries

examples.text: We want a more prosperous world, with more shared development and the freedom to be entrepreneurial and to innovate, create and trade. The development of science and knowledge and the rejection of obscurantism are always the basis for development and the improvement of living conditions. The digital economy and the artificial-intelligence revolution bring with them fears and uncertainties, but above all they offer new opportunities for a better world, if those advances are designed to serve everyone.

First, we must respond to those who feel that the global economy is not working for them; the pace of globalization that has left too many people behind; the fear that our children and grandchildren may lack the education and skills to secure the jobs of tomorrow; and the risk that technological change could become a source of inequality and division rather than the greatest opportunity in history. In the United Kingdom we are driving investment in industries of the future to create new jobs, from low-carbon technologies to artificial intelligence. We are investing in education and skills so that workers are ready to make the most of the opportunities that lie ahead. And we are making sure people play by the rules so that business and innovation is celebrated for creating jobs, not demonized because of grievances over tax not paid or rights not respected.

One way forward that Malta advocates is the harnessing of new technologies, which offer endless possibilities. We are currently in exciting technological times. With the lightning pace of current technological advances, each incredible piece of innovation could hold a new solution to problems that may have persisted for decades — from advanced robotics and artificial intelligence to 3D printing and the Internet of things.

Seventh, technology and innovation are key to reshaping our States and societies. We must strike a prudent balance between guarding against the misuse of emerging technologies and facilitating access to them on the part of developing countries. It is essential to develop universally agreed legal frameworks in the area of cybersecurity, lethal autonomous weapons systems, artificial intelligence and the weaponization of outer space.

Nevertheless, big data, artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things are concepts — terms — that only a part of the world can experience. Not everyone can be operated on by a robot. Inequality includes technological inequality. Fighting technological inequality is also a Sustainable Development Goal.

Artificial intelligence — what will it mean? Helpful robots washing and caring for an ageing population? Or pink-eyed terminators sent back from the future to cull the human race? What will synthetic biology stand for — restoring our livers and our eyes with miracle regeneration of the tissues, like some fantastic hangover cure? Or will it bring terrifying limbless chickens to our tables? Will nanotechnology help us to beat disease, or will it leave tiny robots to replicate in the crevices of our cells?

The Philippines is preparing for the future by laying a governance framework that will enable us to harness the power of renewable energy, develop the capacity to utilize life sciences such as medicine and virology, pursue digital solutions towards a more modern economy and expand our presence in outer space. But we also need to update the global structures that facilitate international cooperation on the peaceful uses of nuclear energy, biology and chemistry, to name but a few. At the same time, we need new structures to govern rapid advances in other areas. We need to start by defining the norms of responsible behaviour in cyberspace and outer space and forming legal rules that will prevent the weaponization of artificial intelligence.

The role that artificial intelligence (AI) and generative artificial intelligence will play in our world must be for good purposes and not evil, but if we are to ensure that is the case, then an appropriate framework for regulatory action must be put in place. We therefore support the actions of the Secretary- General, recognizing that the question will come one day from some, as to whether we sought to preserve our democracy or whether we allowed it to crumble and whether we have failed ourselves as individual citizens of the world. We ask that question recognizing that AI is not in the immediate focal point of many because the drama and the crises that surround climate are taking up all of the oxygen, literally, in the world.

We recognize that while, of course, every nation will want to protect its own interests and strategic advantage, the most important actions we will take will be international. In fact, because tech companies and non-State actors often have country-sized influence and prominence in AI, that challenge requires a new form of multilateralism — because it is only by working together that we will make AI safe for everyone. Our first ever AI summit, in November, will kick-start that process, with a focus on frontier technology.

Building that capacity in liberal, democratic countries is important. Many world-beating technologies were developed in nations where expression flows openly and ideas are exchanged freely. A culture of rules and transparency is essential to creativity and innovation, and it is just as essential to making AI safe.

Perhaps the most exciting thing is that AI can be a democratizing tool open to everyone. Just as we have seen digital adoption sweep across the developing world, AI has the potential to empower millions of people in every part of our planet, giving everyone, wherever they are, the ability to be part of this revolution. AI can and should be a tool for all. Yet any technology that can be used by all can also be used for ill. We have already seen the dangers AI can pose: teens hacking individuals’ bank details, terrorists targeting Government systems, cybercriminals duping voters with deepfakes and bots, even States suppressing their peoples. But our focus on the risks has to include the potential of agentic frontier AI, which at once surpasses our collective intelligence and defies our understanding. Indeed, many argue that the technology is like no other in the sense that its creators themselves do not even know how it works. They cannot explain why it does what it does, and they cannot predict what it will or will not do. The principal risks of frontier AI will therefore come from misuse, misadventure or misalignment with human objectives. Our efforts need to pre-empt those possibilities and to come together to agree a shared understanding of those risks. That is what the AI summit that the United Kingdom is hosting in November will seek to achieve.

Despite the entreaties we saw from some experts earlier in the year, I do not believe we can hold back the tide. There is no future in which that technology does not develop at an extraordinary pace. And although I applaud leading companies’ efforts to put safety at the heart of their development and their voluntary commitments that provide guardrails against unsafe deployment, the starting gun has been fired on a globally competitive race in which individual companies, as well as countries, will strive to push the boundaries as far and fast as possible. Indeed, the stated aim of those companies is to build superintelligence, AI that strives
to surpass intelligence in every possible way. Some people working on that think it is just a few years away.

Even what would seem, at a superficial glance, a tool that could improve the well-being of humankind, at a closer look can turn out to be a risk. Let us just consider artificial intelligence. The applications of that new technology may offer great opportunities in many fields, but we cannot pretend to not understand its enormous inherent risks. I am not sure if we are adequately aware of the implications of technological development, whose pace is much faster than our capacity to manage its effects. We were used to progress that aimed to optimize human capacities, while today we are dealing with progress that risks replacing human

capacities, because, if, in the past, such replacement focused on physical tasks so that humans could dedicate themselves to intellectual and organizational work, today the human intellect risks being replaced, with consequences that could be devastating, particularly for the job market. More and more people will no longer be necessary in a world ever-dominated by disparities and by the concentration of power and wealth in the hands of the few.

One of the biggest drivers of mental health worries is fear of the future. Indeed, none of us can feel secure about our lives if we do not feel secure about what is coming tomorrow. Right now, one of the biggest fears many have is of technology. We have lived through two decades of unprecedented change, from the basic mobile phone and text messaging to smart phones and face recognition. It can often seem like society has lost control and that the technology itself is in charge. And now, with the advent of generative artificial intelligence (AI), the risk is that this seems truer than ever. How we feel about our futures is, unfortunately, not helped by lurid media headlines about the machines taking over, spreading fear about AI taking jobs and rendering human effort obsolete. Let us be clear — AI will have a huge impact on all aspects of society, but let us also be clear that if as leaders we take the right decisions, that impact on our societies can be a positive one.

Again, as with trade, the answer is not to try and turn the clock back, to close our eyes to the inevitable and hope it will go away. Instead, the answer is to get the future right, to take the decisions now so that we can harness the power of AI for the public and common good, not fear it as a coming catastrophe. In Malta, we are already doing just that. We are already seeing how AI can enhance public services, improving lives for all citizens. We have six pilot projects covering areas from health care to traffic management. We are taking ownership through leadership, not trying to ignore the future. Naturally, however, there is a limit to what any one country especially a small one, can do. To make AI a global good, we need global action. Malta stands resolutely behind efforts to increase and enhance international cooperation on AI. Technology is changing too fast, and its potential is so vast, that failing to work together is no longer an option.

Other, newer technological developments also pose profound challenges in balancing the potential of their peaceful use with the threat of catastrophic harm if their development and military use is left unchecked. We must commit to international rules and limits on autonomous weapon systems and establish clear norms to address responsible use of other new and emerging

technologies, including artificial intelligence, as well as the continued peaceful use of outer space. We must also confront digital challenges, including cyberthreats and online extremism through smart coalitions, in which Governments work effectively with civil society and industry.

Although this evolution has enabled us to realize many wishes, it has come at a cost for the people of the world, our planet and its resources. The average life expectancy and standard of living for the majority of humanity have risen, and this has clearly manifested itself in population growth. Nevertheless, poverty and unemployment rates have also increased, and there is a growing awareness of the lack of justice in wealth distribution, in addition to the dire consequences for the environment. In areas such as genetics and artificial intelligence, the possibilities for realizing the well-being of all humanity are increasing. But the gap between possibility and reality is also widening. However, as those possibilities are unfolding in the same era, there are peoples who are grappling with child labour, starvation, unemployment and civil wars, while developed countries guard their borders against the influx of refugees fleeing this suffering, as if the peoples of the earth are living in two different eras.

It is incumbent on us to keep pace with scientific and technological development, encourage it in our countries and encourage barriers between countries in this field to be removed. At the same time, it is not plausible to ignore the worsening risks in terms of reality falsification, invasion of personal privacy, educational process disruption through the facilitation of plagiarism, and the spiralling effect of disinformation and ploys aimed at deception.

Therefore, in addition to the necessity of cooperation and investment in developing those technologies, we reiterate the call for unifying efforts to prevent the misuse of cyberspace and regulate this vital aspect, based on the provisions of international law.

Thirdly, in the midst of the digital revolution and especially the advent of artificial intelligence (AI), we must not only prepare for the risks of those technologies but also distribute their benefits more fairly. In the past year, generative AI such as ChatGPT has captured the popular imagination. But we are actually already on the verge of the next stage: AI agents with the ability to negotiate and transact with each other and humans, and often we will not be able to tell the difference. That has profound implications on all our societies, our politics and economies everywhere. And autonomous weapons systems without human fingers on the triggers are already with us — witness the wars around us. As Secretary-General António Guterres said at the opening of the General Assembly this week,

During the Cold War, the sense of mutually assured destruction imposed mutual restraint — although we now know that there were in fact several close shaves. That spectre of nuclear escalation has not disappeared. Yet the advent of artificial intelligence in conflict situations has actually increased the risks exponentially. We therefore must start an inclusive global dialogue, and we must start it at the United Nations. We need to urgently consider the oversight of such systems and the necessary precautions to avoid miscalculations. That is just one of the many facets to consider as we focus our minds on how to harness the potential and manage the risk of AI. Singapore welcomes the Secretary-General’s decision to convene a high-level advisory body on AI to explore those critical issues.

When we lose trust, we attack the very foundations of organized society in our international community. I am afraid that in our digital age, part of the problem of losing trust lies with science and technology. Inventions are meant to advance humankind. Social media was not invented to disconnect us, but too often it does exactly that. Artificial intelligence can be useful, but it can also be dangerous. In that regard, I applaud the Secretary- General’s resolve to form a high-level advisory body on

artificial intelligence. We need to find a way to govern the development of new technologies, including artificial intelligence, in a way that does not impede economic, development, social and research opportunities and does not put us at risk. The answer should be a humancentric and human rights-based approach to the full life cycle of technologies, encompassing their design, development and application as well as their decline. The Global Digital Compact should be centred on that notion. Things can be done, but we will need all actors, including private companies, to be on board with an honest and meaningful commitment.

A few days ago, we learned about the seven key recommendations of the Secretary-General’s High-level Advisory Body on Artificial Intelligence. We must support those recommendations and move forward with that common effort so as to ensure that decisions about artificial intelligence are not left in the hands of a few and that its development is carried out in an ethical and responsible manner for the benefit of all humankind.

The power of AI seems limitless, a technology with the potential to change our world in a way that will probably surpass the advent of the personal computer, the launch of the mobile phone or the birth of the worldwide web. Like steam or electricity before it, AI as a general technology presents a huge opportunity to transform for good the way we live, collaborate and progress as humankind. If used correctly, it could very well be driving solutions across science, climate change, research and development and medicine. For our Governments, AI has enormous power to enhance productivity, facilitate more effective decision-making and deliver more efficient and higher-impact public services. It is indeed a game-changer. However, AI also has the potential to do extraordinary harm. Unchecked, and in the hands of malign actors, AI could yet become a weapon of control in an uncertain world order. We are already seeing how generative AI is used to create more and more convincing deepfakes, designed to spread misinformation and disinformation.

It is not lost on me, standing here, in this Assembly, created to protect peace and security and promote global dialogue, that our world is being shaped by transnational actors in the form of a few very large technology companies, with more economic muscle than most of the countries represented here. This is leading to an imbalance that we must address. Those driving the technologies that are fundamentally reshaping societies are essentially not accountable, and that needs to change. They, like us, in the end have a responsibility towards humankind. Unlike with climate change, on which we continue to convene globally to discuss national contributions, every year, within the context of a global problem, with AI there is no such framework. The European Union is trying to rectify that but, just as with climate, the EU alone cannot address this challenge. And here I would like to praise the final report, “Governing AI for Humanity”, presented just a few days ago by the High-Level Advisory Body on Artificial Intelligence, established by the Secretary- General. The recommendations of this report can truly contribute to an agile and adaptable regime of global governance of AI that helps to showcase the benefits of AI and address its risks.

Bluntly, if both the Pact for the Future (resolution 79/1) and the Global Digital Compact (ibid., annex I), which we adopted this week, are to have any effect, then we may need to put the regulation and application of AI on a global footing. Eventually, what we may need is a conference of the parties for AI, with the participation not just of countries but also of the global technology companies.

This is an issue of the outmost urgency for one additional reason, and let me conclude with that. We are already witnessing the adverse effects of digital technology and AI-driven algorithms on the mental health of our children and our teenagers. It took more than a quarter of a century for campaigners to install seat belts in cars, despite the fact that all the evidence pointed to belts saving lives. We are in a similar situation today when it comes to children and teenagers and their use of digital and social media platforms. Every day, children around the world are being exposed to content that exacerbates feelings of loneliness and unrealistic standards of beauty. Frequently, our teenagers are pulled into extremist echo chambers. Bullying, once contained to the real world, now has its virtual twin. It follows children home from school and materializes on phones and tablets in bedrooms. Social media algorithms are constantly improved by AI to keep children online for the maximum amount of time and away from the real world of unsupervised play, and all for the purpose

of making money. Countless studies have shown that heavy use of social media is linked to depression, feelings of isolation, sleep deprivation and addiction. The brains of our children are being rewired, and their development changed on an almost unimaginable scale. Yet we do nothing, or very little.

That is why I applaud initiatives such as the one announced by Australia for putting an age limit on social media use, with age verification technologies that cannot be circumvented. Others should follow suit. Technology companies must come to the table and show that they will take tangible and measurable action and prioritize safety over profits. If they do not, pragmatic solutions like banning devices in our schools — which Greece has implemented as of this year — will be complemented by harsher regulatory responses. Digital technology is no different than any other industry that needs to operate under health and safety regulations. The overarching principle, the golden standard, is one and the same: do no harm.

We are witnessing the dawn of the age of artificial intelligence (AI). By now, the promises and the perils of AI are well known to all of us. We need to empower innovation in AI, whilst installing global guardrails to protect human safety, human dignity and values. Therefore, initiating a dialogue on the global governance of AI is imperative. Singapore welcomes the report of the High-Level Advisory Body on AI, and we commit to working with all United Nations Members to further develop those recommendations.
In the years ahead, there may well be no greater test of our leadership than how we deal with AI.

In our National Health Service, AI mammogram trials double the speed of diagnosis. And AI research tools are unlocking new drug combos to fight cancer. On the horizon, the promise of fusion power, powering limitless servers through quantum computing, enabling ever stronger AI, could unleash ever more advanced biotech. This is the defining opportunity of our generation, and we must run towards it with hope. I believe in this promise. I believe in our UN values, which is why this promise must now be shared. We are witnessing a truly historic surge in investment in AI. This investment promises outstanding productivity gains and with it, growth of historic proportions. Yet while this promise may well be diffuse, for now it remains concentrated. But there's not just possibility on the technological frontier. There are profound challenges as well, as AI is being used to consolidate repression, fuel disinformation, empower criminals across the internet. Authoritarian states, notably Russia, are manipulating large-scale, large model language models so that chatbots answer in the voice of their propaganda across the world. Organised crime is using AI to supercharge their scams, deceiving victims on an unprecedented scale. This is the truth. AI can empower freedom or it can entrench repression. AI can empower truth or it can entrench lies. AI can empower law or it can empower crime. Only by cooperation together can we set artificial intelligence on the right millennia-defining course. So my question is this, how can we most effectively share the glittering prizes of this new era across our global community? Well, this is how. We must invest, invest, invest. We must partner, partner, partner. Because without a concerted effort, we risk a world of ever deeper inequality, where the benefits of this technology fail to reach those who need it most. That revolution in healthcare, that revolution in education, that revolution in opportunity, this we must share. This is the world we face, and we take it and its challenges as it is. But never lose sight of the world as it can be.
